Treat visual interface design as a critical, unique communication discipline conducted alongside interaction and industrial design, not as afterthought skinning: place aesthetics within a functional framework driven by user-experience and business goals, and match the visual structure to the logical structure of the users' mental models and the program's behavior so the display communicates behavior clearly.

Make every functional and data element a concrete representation that responds to a specific earlier requirement, so that each aspect of the product traces back to a usage scenario or business goal; comprehensively catalog the data objects, expect one requirement to need several interface elements, and ground the design in realistic business, brand, technical, and customer requirements.

Embody four design values in every solution: ethical (do no harm and improve human situations), purposeful (help users achieve goals and accommodate their contexts and limitations), pragmatic (help the organization and meet business and technical requirements), and elegant (the simplest complete solution with internal coherence that supports cognition and emotion).

Aim for elegance that stimulates and supports the user both cognitively and emotionally in whatever context they are in, which is broader and more appropriate than appealing to the single narrow emotion of desire.

Use design patterns to capture and generalize useful solutions, recording each pattern's context, examples, common features, and rationale, but treat them as neither recipes nor plug-and-play components since context is decisive and a general style guide can never replace a context-specific solution; build a mental catalog of interaction patterns to avoid reinventing the wheel.

Make platform and posture among the first design decisions: choose the platform to balance persona needs against business and technical constraints, and set the product's posture, its behavioral stance reflecting how much attention the user devotes, from the usage context rather than the designer's taste, since look-and-feel is a behavioral choice; define an overall posture plus per-feature postures and make hardware platform decisions in concert with and after interaction design.

Make transient-posture applications simple, clear, and obvious, limited to a single window and view with instructions built into the surface and taking no more space than needed, and give them a memory so they relaunch to their previous size, position, and configuration; treat dialog boxes and the interactive parts of daemonic applications as transient, showing a daemon icon only for continuous useful status and providing a control panel plus inline access.

Deliver application-quality interaction design when complex behavior runs in a browser: know the Web spectrum of informational, transactional, and application, set an informational site's sovereign-versus-transient balance by visit frequency, optimize for common display sizes, avoid forcing unnecessary navigation since perceived load time tracks goal achievement more than actual time, do not assume Web apps are easier to build or more usable for free, and design sovereign Web applications like desktop applications.

Design embedded systems by their guiding principles: do not think of the product as a computer or bring desktop idioms to it, design the hardware and software interface together from a goal-directed and ergonomic perspective, let environmental context drive the design, use modes judiciously, limit the scope to a specific set of tasks done well, balance navigation against display density, and limit and simplify input.

Consider a non-browser Internet-enabled native application when the browser's constraints would hurt the experience, and design devices that share information with a desktop as satellites or extensions that provide key functions where the desktop is unavailable.

Design kiosks for infrequent, often one-time public users without keyboards: optimize for first-time use with a transient posture, distinguish transactional kiosks that let users reach a specific goal fast from explorational kiosks that must engage through an interesting experience, show process orientation and escape hatches, plan placement and wayfinding with industrial design, and keep touch targets large with sparing text input and no drag or scroll, keeping hardware-button mappings consistent.

For television, automotive, appliance, and audible interfaces, match the context: make TV interfaces readable across the room with simple five-way navigation and organize multi-device control around user activities rather than device functions; for cars minimize hands-off-wheel time with consistent layout, direct labeled mappings, single-press mode switching, and non-distracting audible feedback; make appliances transient and simple with familiar hardware controls; and for audible interfaces organize by mental model with common options first, signposting available functions and always offering a way back, to the top, and to a human.

Design to promote and enhance flow, the state of deep, productive concentration, and avoid any flow-disturbing behavior, remembering that the ultimate interface for most purposes is no interface at all, that well-orchestrated interfaces are transparent, and that harmonious interaction cannot be reduced to fixed numeric rules but depends on what the user is trying to accomplish.

Follow users' mental models by organizing and indexing information the way the target user thinks, and pursue less is more by constantly reducing interface elements without reducing capability and avoiding complex-but-not-powerful silos, since minimalism depends on a clear understanding of purpose, though reduction is a balancing act because excessive visual simplicity can create cognitive complexity.

Enable users to direct rather than forcing them to discuss: make the ideal interaction like using a tool, where the user gives direction and gets direct feedback, not a dialogue where the software interrogates the user, since the best flow-inducing interfaces have plentiful and sophisticated direct-manipulation idioms.
Keep tools close at hand, on palettes or toolbars for beginners and intermediates and via keyboard for experts, selectable in a single click or keystroke, and never make the user put tools away.

Do not force physically awkward idioms: because the menu is beginners' primary control yet is hard to operate (requiring click-and-drag), support single-click menu operation and provide an alternative non-drag idiom such as a toolbar button for any function used more than rarely; keep the working set of modal palette tools small, since selecting and deselecting them does not scale for intermediates; and give a charged cursor a clear visual indication of its modal state and a good cancel idiom, allowing either a single click for a default-sized object or a drag-rectangle for a custom size.

Design toolbars to give experienced users fast, visible, immediate access to frequently used functions rather than duplicating the descriptive menu: use images on toolbars and text on menus deliberately, since text is precise but slow (suiting teaching) while a pictograph is ambiguous until learned but then recognized fast (suiting quick access); a butcon's icon need only be recognizable once learned, with its purpose taught through ToolTips (well-timed with about a one-second lag) rather than by labeling it with both text and image, which costs too many pixels; and disable inapplicable toolbar controls by graying them out rather than making them disappear, because users remember toolbar layouts by position.
Provide modeless feedback by building status and effect information into the structure of the interface rather than interrupting the user with a modal dialog.

Prefer modal dialogs where a dialog is used, because they are easiest for users to understand — clearly saying to stop and deal with this now, since freezing application state is what makes them simpler — while modeless dialogs are harder to design and use because the selection can change during their lifetime and their scope is unclear; almost never use a system-modal dialog that halts the entire system (reserve it for catastrophic occurrences); and when a modeless dialog is used, visually differentiate it from modal dialogs and give it a single, consistently placed Close button that is never disabled and never relabeled, relying on the application-wide Undo rather than a Cancel.

Keep users constantly informed with rich visual modeless feedback — information about the status and attributes of processes and objects that is rich, visual, and always displayed without a mode shift, the way a car dashboard is — to help users avoid mistakes and all but eliminate dialogs; recognize that such feedback is not for beginners because it takes work to discover and decode, so keep menus and dialogs as support and make any feedback used to warn of serious trouble extraordinarily clear; and prefer positive audible feedback (a success sound whose absence signals a problem) over negative beeps that act as insulting public alarms.

Design for the probable and provide for the possible, segregating the two so that the readiness to handle improbable edge cases is not rendered directly into the interface beside constantly used controls.
Contextualize quantitative information so it answers the question compared to what and shows the data visually, relegating exact numbers to supporting labels with reasonable, consistent precision.

Avoid unnecessary reporting and never stop the proceedings to report normalcy, instead doing the work, issuing reassuring clues, and taking a good-enough first step the user can adjust rather than requiring the user to direct every action in advance.

Do not stop the proceedings with idiocy: eliminate high-excise error and confirmation dialogs, allow input wherever you have output so a user can change a displayed value in place, and root out common excise traps such as forcing window switches, remembering file locations, reentering settings, asking permission, or confirming actions.

Do, don't ask: give software the courage of its convictions backed by user research rather than interrupting with alerts and confirmation dialogs, because confirmations reflect the implementation model, pass the buck to users, and only work when unexpected (routine ones get dismissed by rote like the boy who cried wolf, so a real danger warning is ignored) — instead make all actions reversible, even deleting or overwriting a file by moving it to a holding area first, and let the user issue Undo on the rare occasion an action was wrong, keeping them informed through modeless feedback rather than stopping the proceedings.

Avoid blank slates by making a statistically reasonable assumption the user can adjust, asking forgiveness rather than permission, and differentiate command from configuration so invoking a function performs it with previous or standard settings while a separate configuration command exposes the options, because users invoke a command about ten times for every configuration.

Provide choices rather than asking questions, putting immediate access on toolbar buttons and configuration on menu items, because a question puts the software in a superior interrogating position, products that ask fewer questions appear smarter and more considerate, and people treat interactive software as if it were a person whose projected personality matters.

Hide the ejector-seat levers: keep configuration facilities that cause major visual dislocation or irreversible action away from inexperienced users and ensure they can never be triggered accidentally during a minor adjustment.

Optimize for responsiveness and accommodate latency, communicating unavoidable delays and letting users cancel and do other work, and respect the response-time thresholds where up to 0.1 second feels instantaneous, up to 1 second responsive, up to 10 seconds needs a progress bar, and beyond 10 seconds should run in the background with status, estimated time, and a cancel mechanism.

Eliminate excise, the extra cognitive and physical work that serves the tools or outside agents rather than the user's goal: remove pure excise, do not weld on training wheels, judge visual excise from over-reliance on metaphor and ornament, and determine whether a function is excise by comparing it to persona goals, while neither removing excise merely for power users nor forcing them to pay the price of beginners' help.

Treat navigation as largely excise and minimize it, recognizing that navigation among multiple windows, views, or pages is the most disorienting kind, which sovereign applications avoid by placing all main interactions in a single primary view with panes.

Use adjacent panes to reduce navigation, placing panes that support drag-and-drop next to each other, avoid splitting one facility across tabbed panes since that increases excise, reserve tabs for a multi-document work area or mutually exclusive supporting panes, group frequently used tools spatially while reserving menus for infrequent commands, and minimize scrolling.

Improve navigation by reducing the number of places a user must go, keeping windows, views, panes, and controls to the minimum needed, providing signposts as persistent objects, overviews, appropriate control-to-function mapping, interface inflection, and by avoiding hierarchies.

Avoid multi-window navigation schemes for moving between programs: the overlapping-sheets window metaphor does not scale beyond about three applications and causes lost-window confusion, and multiple windows sharing a small screen (overlapping or tiled) is not a good general solution, so prefer full-screen applications with a minimal switching mechanism such as a taskbar; inside a sovereign application, however, multipaned windows that display related information in adjacent panes reduce navigation and window-management excise to almost nil and are practically a requirement.

Make the normal state of a sovereign application a maximized full-screen window, with little reason to pluralize it except to support switching or dragging data between programs, and use a multiple-document interface only when users genuinely need multiple related views together in one environment, not when it forces them to manage little windows inside a big one or destroys orientation permanency through changing menus — often clean full-window switching is better.

Avoid presenting abstract hierarchies, which are very difficult for users to navigate, and instead render a storage structure as monocline grouping the way users imagine it while providing the search and access tools that only a deep hierarchy offers, so information is brought to the user rather than requiring deep-tree navigation.

Make a product considerate by embodying the traits of a caring person: take an interest and remember what the user tells it, defer and submit to the user, be forthcoming, use common sense, be conscientious about the larger goal, keep quiet about its own problems, be perceptive by remembering preferences, be self-confident rather than asking Are you sure while staying ready to undo, fail gracefully, know when to bend the rules with suspense states, and take responsibility for the work it hands to other devices.
Make a product smart by having it work hard even when conditions are difficult and users are not busy, putting the many idle CPU cycles to work proactively rather than leaving the processor idle.

Give a product a memory across sessions and exploit task coherence, the fact that users' goals and tasks are similar day to day, to predict behavior and greatly reduce the questions it asks, following the rule that if it is worth the user entering, it is worth the application remembering.

Apply memory concretely: use the previous setting as the default and remember options until manually changed without re-offering turned-off features, remember file locations per file type and window position, remember repeated action patterns, remember essentially everything since storage is cheap, remember deduced information for silent reasonableness checks, persist the undo stack across sessions, and auto-fill past entries to reduce errors.

Predict and act using decision-set reduction by remembering more than the single last choice, preference thresholds by not asking for successively detailed decisions but assuming and remembering them, and the mostly-right-most-of-the-time approach of doing the most appropriate thing and letting users override or undo it, given a sufficiently easy undo.

Give metaphors, especially physical and spatial ones, an extremely limited place in software design, and choose among the three interface paradigms by preferring the idiomatic, based on learning how to accomplish things, over the difficult implementation-centric and risky metaphoric paradigms; avoid implementation-centric and org-chart-centric interfaces that force users to understand internal structure, because most people would rather be successful than knowledgeable.

Give metaphors an extremely limited place in interface design: they do not scale as a process grows in complexity, depend on cultural associations the user may not share, and offer only a small first-use learnability boost while permanently limiting software power for the intermediates users soon become.

Never bend the interface to fit a metaphor; use a metaphor only when a truly appropriate and powerful one falls in your lap, because good metaphors are hard to find for software's processes and relationships, global metaphors add navigation overhead, and extending a metaphor tempts you toward an obsolete mechanical model — the Macintosh succeeded through overall design detail, not its desktop metaphor.

Design idiomatically: base the interface on simple, nonmetaphorical visual and behavioral idioms that the mind learns quickly from a single exposure, recognizing that most elements of so-called intuitive GUIs (windows, close boxes, scrollbars, drop-downs, the mouse) are actually learned idiomatically rather than intuited metaphorically.

Structure the interaction vocabulary as an inverted pyramid — a small set of primitives (pointing, clicking, dragging), compounds built from them, and domain-specific idioms built from compounds — and restrict the number of atomic primitives, because the more atomic elements a vocabulary has the harder it is to learn.

Honor manual affordances: use simulated-3D shading to signal that an element can be manipulated, but because a virtual affordance shows only that a control is manipulable and not what it does, always label controls with text or icons, and deliver on the contract an affordance makes by responding visually when actuated and doing the reasonable work the control's legend describes — never bait-and-switch.

Let the shape, behavior, and affordance of controls drive the visual style so aesthetic considerations never interfere with meaning or the ability to interact, controlling stylized elements especially carefully in sovereign applications.

Make direct manipulation succeed through rich visual feedback: provide a visual representation of the objects of concern, visible gestural mechanisms for acting on them instead of text commands, and immediately visible results; render data, objects, controls, and cursors with enough graphic detail to be manipulable, since users can directly manipulate only what is displayed; and decide from the personas' skills and contexts what should be manipulated directly versus handled more indirectly, because direct-manipulation idioms are easily taught and seldom forgotten yet can demand motor coordination.

Group, align, and lay out with structure: group related elements by proximity and whitespace rather than heavy bounding boxes, align every element with as many others as possible on a modular grid whose spacing is multiples of one atomic unit, structure an efficient top-to-bottom left-to-right path for the eye with balanced visual weight, and use the squint test to reveal hierarchy, grouping, and balance problems.

Communicate function and consequences visually by rendering an illustrative picture, diagram, or preview of the result in addition to text, as with Print Preview, because a visualization conveys consequences that words alone cannot.

Keep verbal, visual, and behavioral brand messages consistent because brand value is the sum of all interactions people have with a company: a pleasing design earns a strong first impression (the Aesthetic-Usability Effect makes it feel easier to use), but long-term brand equity is built only by delivering behavior consistent with that impression, and a stunning look counts for nothing if the user cannot get the answer she needs.

Minimize and optimize interface text: never set it in all capitals (which defeats shape-based letter recognition), represent what an object is with a visual symbol and use text only to tell which particular object it is, and where text is needed use a crisp sans-serif at 10 pixels or larger with roughly 80 percent contrast, the fewest words needed for clear meaning, and no nonstandard abbreviations.

Avoid the common color misuses: too many colors (search degrades at about seven or more), saturated complementary pairs that cause chromostereopsis, excessive saturation, inadequate contrast when figure and ground differ only in hue, and inattention to color-blindness, which affects roughly ten percent of males.

Design storage and retrieval from the users' mental models and usage contexts rather than exposing the file system: because storage and retrieval need not be linked digitally as they are physically, do not hand users the storage system as the retrieval system, and since positional (where it was left) and identity (its name) retrieval both burden memory, provide associative, attribute-based retrieval so users can find documents by their contents and meaningful properties expressed the way they think.

Reduce the burden of organizing files: automatically remember many document attributes (creating application, format, size, edit/print/email history, usage frequency), return search results fast by indexing content during idle time, and also let users tag or manually assign attributes to form a folksonomy that fills gaps and defines dynamically overlapping sets, which is especially valuable in collaborative contexts.

Separate the storage system from the retrieval system rather than forcing users to conform to a rigid relational schema: keep records in a database-like digital soup that accepts any record and returns a token, build retrieval as an unlimited number of attribute indices each keyed to one concept, fill those indices both by automatic extraction and by easy manual pointers, and never demand that users configure their information in advance, because they rarely can express their needs ahead of time and often change their minds.

Present storage according to the user's single-document mental model rather than the file system's implementation model of two copies (one in memory, one on disk) that both belong to the application: hide the file system's existence, use a unified file model that treats the document as one thing and leaves disk/memory writing to the file system, and avoid the Save As trap that conflates naming and placing a file, cannot rename or relocate the current document, and can silently discard recent changes.

Prefer natural language output over natural language input for attribute-based queries: give users an array of bounded, cascading controls that read like an English sentence and let them assemble a valid query from a grammar of choices, sparing them Boolean and SQL syntax, because reliable natural language input is beyond typical commercial systems; map the grammars in advance and attend to localization for languages with different word order.

Model Undo the least like its implementation and the most like the user's mental model, because Undo exists exclusively for humans, who make mistakes: treat everything the user does as valid and reasonable rather than as error, recognize that Undo's primary purpose is to support exploration (reassuring users and encouraging experimentation), and understand that it serves the necessary condition of trustworthiness rather than directly advancing a goal.

Design Undo to satisfy the several mental models users bring — a panic button, a deleted-data store, a stack of reversible operations — make it a global, program-wide function that undoes the last action however it was performed, keep it available after a document is saved, save the undo buffer with the document, and never hint through visual, audible, or textual cues that Undo signals a user failure.

Exploit richer reversal idioms: treat a paired Undo-Redo as a comparison or what-if tool and consider a single Compare control that follows the user's apply-versus-don't-apply mental model, and offer category-specific incremental Undo (like Backspace undoing only typed characters while ignoring intervening functions), which works because everything is visible and consistent with the user's mental model.

Audit the application for operations that only masquerade as undo-proof (renaming a file) versus those genuinely irreversible (a sent email), making the former undoable; and where business rules or institutional policy forbid undoing an action, still serve human goals by providing a way to reverse or adjust it while leaving an audit trail.

Complement incremental Undo with a browsable deleted-data buffer that lets users recover deleted content directly and randomly rather than reversing every intervening step, and support versioning by letting users snapshot the whole document and later revert from a list of versions annotated with time, author, size, and notes, saving the current state as a new version on revert.

Implement document handling to match the unified model: save automatically on close without a confirmation dialog and at intervals or in the background during a session (keeping an optional manual save), provide an explicit Create a Copy that quietly makes an independently named copy in the same directory, let users rename in place by clicking the title-bar name and put new files somewhere findable like the Desktop, treat storage format as a document property accessed through Document Properties or Export rather than bundled into Save, provide an explicit Abandon Changes or Revert rather than using the file system as a surrogate for Undo, and drop the implementation-model File menu name in favor of the document type or Document.

Recognize that disk technology is a cost compromise and a hack that has shaped software for implementation rather than user purposes, and that although users cannot predict the effects of interaction-paradigm shifts and reject unfamiliar change, they will gladly abandon painful, poorly designed software for easier, better software once it exists — so do not let users' resistance to change veto a genuinely better design.

Never stop a user for missing data: let him enter what he has now and return later, communicating required-but-missing fields through rich modeless feedback rather than blocking his work; and where data truly must be valid, use type-ahead auto-completion or bounded controls (drop-downs, smart-parsing fields) plus unobtrusive modeless feedback so the user stays in control and the application does less policing.

Do not treat all information workers as untrustworthy to guard against the few who are, since that is counterproductive and self-fulfilling — lowering productivity and morale and raising error rates — but instead build fudgeability into rigid systems by making the queue, document, and its position visible and manipulable and allowing records to be held in suspense, and prevent abuse by keeping very detailed records of user actions so full accountability is possible.

Audit, don't edit: an application's duty to report errors extends to other applications, not to users, so accept whatever the user tells it (treating the user as always right and their errors as the application's responsibility), make any suspected problem clear unobtrusively and modelessly — highlighting a suspect field the way a speedometer silently reports speed rather than stopping the proceedings with a dialog — while remembering every action, ensuring clean reversibility, and maintaining a clear audit trail rather than jumping in to fix things and subverting the user's intent.

Fully support both mouse and keyboard for all navigation and selection, providing at least one non-mouse alternative for each mouse idiom because many users, especially touch-typists, dislike leaving the keyboard; and design around the cost of transitioning between fine and gross motor skills by placing things used together together and avoiding idioms (like the classic split scrollbar) that force continual motor-skill changes.

Use meta-keys (Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Command) to extend and modify direct-manipulation idioms with cursor hinting that reflects the new function while the key is pressed, and treat double-click as single-click plus action (select then act) while ensuring every double-click idiom has a single-click equivalent, because double-clicking is difficult or impossible for some less-dexterous users.

Make the interpretation of mouse-down and mouse-up rigidly consistent within a product and ideally across the platform: over selectable data, mouse-down should select (since the click may begin a drag and you cannot drag without first selecting); over a control, mouse-down should tentatively propose the action by showing the state transition and mouse-up should commit it, which lets a user bow out of an inadvertent click by moving off the control before releasing.

Visually communicate pliancy so it is obvious which elements are manipulable, informational, or decorative: prefer dynamic hinting (a control gains its affordance as the cursor rolls over it) to reduce persistent clutter, add pliant-response hinting when the mouse is pressed but not released inside a control (a button indenting), which both signals the forthcoming action and forms part of the cancel mechanism, and use cursor hinting for manipulable data and small controls like column dividers and splitters that cannot easily hint at pliancy themselves.

Prefer object-verb command ordering (select the object, then choose the verb) for direct manipulation because it needs no termination, lets a user apply several verbs to one selection, and lets the application show only commands appropriate to the selection; default selection to mutual exclusion, allowing additive selection via a meta-key for discrete data but generally not for contiguous data (where scrolling makes off-screen selections uncontrollable); and make the selection state visually evident and unambiguous without relying on color alone, using handles or a marching-ants marquee for visually rich objects.

Give drag-and-drop precise, positive feedback: have each drop candidate visually indicate its receptivity while the drag cursor identifies the source object (never confusing the two by using the cursor to show drop candidacy), avoid negative feedback like the Not-Permitted symbol that is easily misread as a warning against releasing, drag a transparent outline or thumbnail so the object does not obscure a small target and the cursor hotspot stays visible, show an insertion target such as a caret bar when an object can drop between others, and give clear completion feedback so it is obvious the drop occurred.

Tune drag mechanics to intent: auto-scroll any scrollable drop target starting just inside the window border, ideally at a rate that increases toward the edge with a speed limit and after about a half-second delay so a slow user does not trigger it inadvertently; and when an object can be both selected and dragged, debounce with a drag threshold of about three pixels (treating movement within it as selection), using an axially non-symmetric threshold biased toward the more frequent direction when two drag directions must be distinguished.

Offer a vernier or fine-scrolling mode, activated by a meta-key or arrow keys, for any program that demands precise alignment, and desensitize the mouse on the first vernier keystroke so that releasing the mouse button does not disturb the precise placement.

Support precise object positioning and manipulation: dedicate a specific area such as a title bar to repositioning so the object's drag idiom stays free for other functions (with explicit pliancy hinting), offer a meta-key constrained drag that locks movement to a single axis, assist alignment with guides and dynamic smart guides and snapping, and use resize handles that double as selection indicators (vertex handles for polylines, Bezier handles for curves) — remembering that handles obscure the object they mark, making them poor permanent controls best replaced by frame or corner resizers for windows.

Provide the right specialized manipulation idioms: offer both a bounding-box idiom for proportional scaling and a vertex-editing idiom for fine-tuning a freeform object's shape, since each serves a distinct purpose, and implement object connection (dragging a line or arrow between objects) with rubber-banding feedback, active hinting that highlights valid targets as the connection is dragged over them, and a convenient way to cancel.

For manipulating 3D objects on a 2D screen, treat rich modeless feedback (baseline grids, depth cueing, shadows, poles, color-coded guidelines) as a necessity for conveying position and movement, use multiple viewpoints to aid alignment despite the mental triangulation they require, and address the picking problem of selecting occluded objects with techniques such as a hover menu of candidates, per-facet pliancy hinting, and fluid navigation (mapping zoom and orbit to the scroll wheel) supported by a thumbnail absolute view to keep users oriented.

Do not treat modes as inherently evil in the object-verb world of a GUI, even though they are poisonous on a command line, because the benefit of an interface like MacPaint comes not from modelessness but from the ease of seeing which mode the program is in and changing that mode effortlessly.

Treat each window, pane, or dialog box as a separate room and do not add one unless it serves a purpose existing windows cannot: put functions in the window where they are used, so a task integral to the application's purpose belongs in the main window rather than a dialog (one of the most frequently violated UI principles), reserve a separate room such as a dialog for functions performed outside the user's normal sequence (purging a database, importing clip art), and avoid windows pollution from putting a single function in each dialog, since a goal involves a series of functions whose connections many windows cannot show.

Put primary interactions in the primary window and let dialog boxes play only a secondary role, because forcing users to bounce between the main window and its dialogs leads to fatigue: reserve dialogs for functions out of the main flow — anything confusing, dangerous, dislocating, or rarely used — giving a big friendly Cancel button and room for protective and explanatory information, and use dialogs to gather the controls and information about a single domain object or a single function in one place, reducing the navigation excise of hunting through the interface.

Prefer toolbars, palettes, and sidebars over modeless dialogs, because they are modeless without the conundrums — visually distinct, omnipresent so they need no terminating control, efficient in screen space, and not covering what they operate on; and since repositioning windows is never a user's goal, replace free-floating modeless dialogs (which create window-management excise) with docked palettes, sidebars, task panes, or a properties area that provide the same modeless interactivity while retaining the user's context.

Understand that controls come in four goal-directed flavors — imperative controls that initiate a function, selection controls that choose options or data, entry controls that enter data, and display controls that visually manipulate the program — and remember that a multitude of control-laden dialog boxes does not make a good interface, because standard controls guarantee ease of implementation but not ease of use and must be used judiciously, whereas a direct-manipulation interface consistent with user mental models is harder to build but better.

Make list controls efficient and manipulable: distinguish important items with graphic icons so users find them faster than scanning text, use earmarking (a check box per item) rather than disabling mutual exclusion for multiple selection in a scrollable list, support drag-and-drop from and within lists with auto-scroll, make items editable in place with a discoverable way to add a new entry (a perpetual Click to Add Entry row), and never scroll text horizontally because it hides the first letters of every line and destroys readability.

Favor the combo box — a list combined with an edit field — as a superb, space-efficient single-selection control that is replacing radio-button groups because it shows the current selection without any action, can add items dynamically, and can live permanently on a toolbar or sovereign screen; and use a tree or hierarchy control only when the data is naturally thought of as a hierarchy, because forcing arbitrary data into a treeview hides the more interesting non-hierarchical relationships between objects.

Put knowledge in the program rather than in the user's head: make text edit controls smart enough to recognize appropriate units such as inches or millimeters and let users choose named values like default or best fit from a combo box, and use noneditable display controls for output-only text, because an edit control's system font and white box encourage data entry and mislead users into thinking read-only output is editable.

Display a changeable value in an editable field so users can click and change it directly where it is shown, because separating the mechanism to input a value from the mechanism to output it through a special edit mode is almost always excise.

Handle panes and control details with care: advertise a movable splitter's pliancy with cursor hinting and never let it move so far that a pane's contents become unusable, using a drawer idiom (a pane that opens and closes with a single action) when a pane must collapse entirely or to hold less-frequently-used controls that are most useful in the context of the main work area; and attend to the details of controls, because frustrating controls cause constant low-level annoyance that undermines even an excellent product concept.

Treat menus as a pedagogic vector whose primary role is to teach new users, remind those who have forgotten, and provide access to infrequently used functions — not as the main way normal users perform everyday functions, which toolbars and direct manipulation serve better — so flatten deep sequential menu hierarchies into monocline grouping (aided by dialogs that gather subchoices) to improve scanability, make menu text verbose and jargon-free (Open Report rather than Open) and the menus complete so a scan reveals the program's full scope, and support users moving ad hoc and piecemeal from beginner to expert by reading the menu for unfamiliar functions while invoking familiar ones with memorized shortcuts.

Do not blindly accept the standard File, Edit, and Help menu structure, which reflects implementation-model thinking and names that sound like tools rather than goals; organize menus by users' mental models and a goal-directed structure, naming the primary menu after the document type when appropriate.

Design menu structure and item behavior for clarity: use cascading hierarchical menus only in sophisticated sovereign applications for rarely used functions or as a secondary vector (with a wide movement threshold), avoid adaptive menus that hide infrequent items (which studies show slow users down and which they overwhelmingly dislike), avoid bang/immediate menus whose title executes a function (immediate commands belong on toolbars), gray out inapplicable menu items to improve the menu's teaching value, and use a checkmark item that is clearly checked or unchecked rather than a flip-flop item that shows the state not currently chosen.

Provide multiple parallel command vectors — menus, toolbars, keyboard accelerators, and direct manipulation — so users of different skill sets can command the program the way that suits them, giving immediate vectors to the minimal working set of frequently used functions identified from persona scenarios and pedagogic vectors to beginners, and understanding that information in the world (menus, dialogs) is dependable but slow while information in the head (accelerators) is fast but must be learned, so beginners rely on world vectors and experts increasingly on head vectors; as an exception, deny dangerous commands like Erase All easy parallel vectors and protect them within menus and dialogs like hidden ejector-seat levers.

Build strong keyboard and cross-vector support: show the same identifying icon on a menu item as on its corresponding toolbar butcon so users build a visual language connecting the two, create good keyboard accelerators by following platform standards and assigning them to functions in everyone's daily use (shown to the right of each menu item, triaged by always/never/maybe daily use), and treat access keys or mnemonics as not optional, providing a complete, consistent keyboard equivalent of every menu command.

Build a memorization vector into the interface — a path by which users learn the fast head vector corresponding to each slow world vector — through accelerators shown beside menu items, underlined mnemonics, and a Shortcuts item on the Help menu rather than buried documentation, and show each function's identifying icon on every artifact that deals with it (every menu, butcon, dialog, help text, and printed page), because a memorization vector of consistent visual symbols is the most effective yet underexploited technique.

Design dialog boxes with a strong visual hierarchy, subject-based groupings, and a conventional reading-order layout; have them appear on the topmost layer when instantiated and always give them a clear title, using a verb in a function dialog's title bar (Insert Break rather than Break) and the object's name in a property dialog's title bar so the title matches what the user is actually doing.

Recognize the four goal-directed dialog types — property dialogs to view and change a selected object's attributes, function dialogs to initiate and configure a single function, process dialogs to report a busy internal function, and bulletin dialogs for unrequested messages — separate configuring a function from invoking it while linking them seamlessly (so a routine task need not confront the full complexity of options), and whenever an application begins a perceptibly time-consuming process, inform the user that it is busy but otherwise normal, or the silence will read as rudeness or a crash.

Avoid dialog anti-patterns: never use transitory dialogs that take themselves down for errors or confirmations, because the message must stop the program so the user definitely gets it; minimize bulletin dialogs (errors, alerts, confirmations), which serve the application at the user's expense, unlike requested property and function dialogs; group a tabbed dialog with a meaningful breadth-or-depth rationale and split stacked tabs into several dialogs with fewer tabs each; and treat cascading dialogs (one summoning another with its own OK/Cancel) as confusing symptoms of excessive complexity and structural flaws in the interaction framework.

Understand that error message boxes stop the proceedings with idiocy and mostly report the program's own inability to work flexibly rather than a genuinely serious problem: most bulletins fire when the computer is confused by out-of-bounds or out-of-sequence input rather than a substantive user mistake, so the software should assume the human input is correct and work harder to reconcile it — accepting the transaction with modeless feedback that something is not yet recognized and letting the user supply missing information before the session ends, the way manual systems work — recognizing that error messages do not prevent user errors, they only prevent the program from getting into trouble.

Eliminate error messages by redesigning the software to be immune to the problem and to prevent error conditions from arising — treating an error message as an abnormal idiom of last resort — using bounded controls such as drop-downs and lists so users cannot enter bad values, and making the application smart enough to avoid unnecessary demands by supplying known values itself, remembering prior files, and reading the date from the internal clock.

Favor positive over negative feedback, because people learn better from acknowledged success than from being slapped on the wrist and negative feedback from a machine is humiliating and helps nothing; and treat the ad hoc appearance and disappearance of hardware and networks (printers, drives, wireless connections) as normal behavior rather than an error, having the application do something intelligent like saving locally and synchronizing later.

Distinguish personalization — decorating persistent objects such as colors and non-structural elements, which aids navigation and makes software likable and familiar — from configuration — moving, adding, or deleting persistent objects, which hinders navigation but is desirable for experienced users and necessary for experts: make personalization tools simple, previewable, and above all easy to undo (including a return to factory settings); recognize that most end users will not mind being unable to configure a program if it does its job well, while configuration is critical for rapidly evolving workflows and highly valued by corporate IT buyers; and where a population splits roughly evenly on two idioms, offer both rather than choosing one, ideally so they coexist without a preference setting.

Anticipate globalization: immediate, idiomatic, visual command vectors such as direct manipulation and butcons globalize with relative ease so long as their colors and symbols carry no unintended cultural meaning, whereas pedagogic textual vectors (menu items, labels, ToolTips) are language-dependent and require localization; and when localizing, account for varying text length, difficult alphabetical sorting, and differing date, time, decimal, and calendar formats, translating items holistically so the interface stays coherent as a whole rather than only item by item.

Reduce reliance on documentation through design: offer a gallery of ready-to-use templates so users can pick a premade starting design and make small changes, because a blank slate intimidates most people; and treat online help as a reference tool for perpetual intermediates already using the product who want to expand their horizons, not as a crutch or a resource aimed at beginners, letting good design greatly reduce users' need for help.

Design help as a reference for perpetual intermediates: make the index the priority of any reference document, generating it from an examination of the program and all its features rather than only the help text, with as many synonyms as possible and the goal-directed terms a user would actually search for; include a Shortcuts digest of tools and keyboard commands and an overview describing each feature's scope, effect, power, and trade-offs; and rely on ToolTips as modeless online help, which is incredibly effective, unlike a standard separate help program that covers up the application and cannot point at on-screen objects the way a helpful person would.

Avoid interrogating and anthropomorphic help idioms: wizards violate the principle of providing choices rather than asking questions, treating users as peripheral devices through step-by-step interrogation that devolves into confirmation-clicking, so prefer a simple automatic function that does the job with no questions and lets users adjust the result afterward with standard tools; and avoid anthropomorphic animated help agents, because lifelike characters raise users' expectations of intelligence beyond what they can deliver, making them cloying and distracting when users simply want direct, trustworthy assistance.
